de7_what_it_gets_right.topic: The diagnosis steelmanned: trust, capacity, administrative state, responsiveness, FDR 1933

claims.text: Pew, survey dated 28 Sept 2025: 17% trust the federal government to do what is right always (2%) or most of the time (15%); Democrats 9%, Republicans 26%; NES 1958 73%, 1964 77% (series high)
Gallup July 2025: average confidence across nine institutions tracked since 1979 was 28%, against 48% in 1979; Democrats record low 26%; Republicans 37%

GAO 30 July 2014: CMS developed Healthcare.gov 'without effective planning or oversight practices'; FFM obligations rose from $56M (Sept 2011) to more than $209M (Feb 2014); a replacement contract of $91M (Jan 2014) exceeded $175M by June 2014
GAO 25 Feb 2025: 38 high-risk areas; agencies reported $2.8 trillion in estimated improper payments since 2003; high-risk work produced nearly $759 billion in savings

Kamarck (Brookings, 28 Jan 2025): federal civilian employment 'has stayed the same since the mid-1960s'; 1.1% of population in FY1967, 0.6% in 2018; contractors outnumber federal employees more than two to one (Light); FY2022 contract spending $694.2bn; SSA staff fell from nearly 67,000 (2010) to 56,645 (2024)
CFR pages: 22,877 in 1960; 71,224 in 1975; 157,972 in 2008; 188,346 at end of 2021 (CEI, from Office of the Federal Register data)
Thompson (1980) named 'the problem of many hands' in public office, APSR 74: 905-16
Branham, Soroka and Wlezien: rich and middle-income Americans agree about 90% of the time; when they disagree the rich win 53% of the time, 'only a little more often than the middle'
Gilens and Page (2016) reply: 'we don't believe that any of these critiques, individually or collectively, undermine our central claims'

FDR, 4 March 1933: hoped the 'normal balance of executive and legislative authority' would suffice; only if Congress failed to act and the emergency remained critical would he ask Congress for 'broad Executive power to wage a war against the emergency, as great as the power that would be given to me if we were in fact invaded by a foreign foe'
Emergency Banking Act introduced and passed on 9 March 1933; Title I expanded presidential powers in a banking crisis and retroactively approved the bank holiday
Schechter Poultry v. US, 27 May 1935, unanimous: NIRA codes an unconstitutional delegation of legislative power and beyond the commerce power

FDR's court plan announced 5 Feb 1937 (up to six new justices); Senate Judiciary Committee report called it 'an invasion of judicial power such as has never before been attempted in this country'; Senate shelved it in July 1937

Yarvin (NYT, Jan 2025) paraphrased the 1933 inaugural as FDR saying 'hey, Congress, give me absolute power or I'll take it anyway' and said FDR did take it; also 'it's not even that democracy is bad, it's just that it's very weak'; 'I don't believe in actually voting at all'

Land, Dark Enlightenment p.3: 'winning elections is overwhelmingly a matter of vote buying'; p.6: neocameral transition requires 'the entire social landscape of political bribery (lobbying) is exactly mapped' and converted into 'fungible shares'; 'No voice, free exit'

Gilens and Page (2016 reply): 'Economic elites and interest groups can shape U.S. government policy' while 'Americans who are less well off have essentially no influence over what their government does'

de7_the_other_diagnosis.topic: Same symptoms read the other way: money, technofeudalism, enshittification

claims.text: OpenSecrets 2024 cycle: Musk gave more than $291M to Republican candidates, PACs and outside groups; Timothy Mellon, Miriam Adelson, the Uihleins, Kenneth Griffin and the Yasses each $100M or more on the Republican side; Paul Singer $66.8M; Michael Bloomberg $64M; Dustin Moskovitz $51M

Varoufakis: capitalism 'has not been overthrown but has instead become something else' (technofeudalism); 'cloud capital' extracts rent; users are 'cloud serfs'; reviewer Weatherby 'not convinced' capitalism is dead
ADS 2023 Word of the Year 'enshittification' (Doctorow, Pluralistic): platforms serve users, then exploit them for business customers, then exploit those customers to claw back value, then decline

claims.text: Yarvin (NYT Jan 2025): 'I do a speech sometimes where I'll just read the last 10 paragraphs of FDR's first inaugural address'; 'This is just a picture of FDR acting like a CEO'; 'FDR ran the new deal like a startup'; asked whether FDR took that power: 'Yeah, he did'
Land (p. 3), summarising Lind and the neo-reactionaries: democracy is 'indistinguishable from the expansion of the state'; 'winning elections is overwhelmingly a matter of vote buying'

CNN (30 May 2025), asked how to stop a leader becoming 'the next Hitler or Stalin', Yarvin: 'You need to concentrate that power in a single individual' and 'hope somehow that this is the right individual, or close to the right individual'; monarch accountable to 'some sort of corporate board' 'but not by the average citizen'; CNN reported the 2022 'ninjas' who would 'drop into all the agencies in the executive branch'
